draft.title: Reaction quotient
card: The reaction quotient, Q, has the same form as the equilibrium constant, K. For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, Q = [C]^c[D]^d ÷ [A]^a[B]^b.
Q uses the concentrations at any moment, so it can change as the reaction proceeds. K uses only the concentrations at equilibrium.
If Q is less than K, there are too many reactants and too few products. The net reaction moves forward, towards products, until Q = K.
If Q is greater than K, there are too many products. The net reaction moves in reverse, towards reactants, until Q = K. If Q equals K, the system is at equilibrium.
draft.remember: Compare Q with K: the reaction moves in whichever direction brings Q towards K.

a.q: At a given temperature, a mixture has Q = 0.5 and K = 4.0. What will happen to the mixture?
opts: The net reaction moves forward, forming more products
The net reaction moves in reverse, forming more reactants
The mixture stays the same because it is at equilibrium
The value of K falls until it equals Q
a.why: Q is less than K, so there are too few products compared with equilibrium. The net reaction moves forward until Q rises to equal K. K does not change, because the temperature has not changed.
a.clue: Which way must Q move to reach K?

b.q: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), K = 0.50 at a set temperature. A mixture has [N2] = 1.0 M, [H2] = 2.0 M and [NH3] = 2.0 M. Which statement is correct?
opts: Q = 0.5, so the mixture is at equilibrium
Q = 2.0, so the net reaction moves in reverse
Q = 0.5, so the net reaction moves forward
Q = 2.0, so the net reaction moves forward
b.why: Q = [NH3]^2 ÷ ([N2][H2]^3) = 4.0 ÷ (1.0 × 8.0) = 0.50. This equals K, so the mixture is at equilibrium. The tempting answers come from forgetting to raise concentrations to the power of their coefficients.
b.clue: Raise each concentration to the power of its coefficient, then compare Q with K.

a.best: The net reaction moves forward, forming more products

b.best: Q = 0.5, so the mixture is at equilibrium

problems.detail: The why says the tempting answers all come from forgetting to raise concentrations to their powers. That only explains Q = 2.0 if the H2 cube is dropped (4.0 ÷ (1.0 × 2.0)); inverting the ratio also gives 2.0. The option 'Q = 0.5, so the net reaction moves forward' comes from misreading the Q–K comparison, not from forgetting powers.

check.summary: Both questions are correct and each has one right answer. The only issue is that the why for (b) misdescribes where the wrong options come from.
